Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:21: In this same manner King David, peace be upon him, said, "When I consider Your heavens, the work of Your fingers, the moon..." (Psalms 8:4). The intent is that King David, peace be upon him, did not look at the heavens in their physicality visible to the eyes, but by looking at their inner spirituality, which is "the work of Your fingers," the ten supernal sefirot; this is likewise the meaning of "the moon and stars which You have established" — it was by their establishment that he looked, for through the establishment of the lower one the work of the supernal one is discerned and recognized.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:22: Regarding the rectification of "humility of eye," one should conduct himself in the attributes of Rav [Judah], peace be upon him, one of whose ten qualities was that he would not look beyond four cubits, and his face was turned to the ground and not to the sides, so as not to see any transgression.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:23: Further, it seems to me that in looking at the ground, he should think that he is dust and shall return to dust, and not think of the transient, perishable matters of this world. A person must practice this rectification while in his own home, so that he becomes trained, when he walks in the marketplace or a place where matters of nakedness are found, not to look at them. And if he is trained within his home not to look beyond four cubits, so as not to remove the fear from himself, thinking as if he stands before the King, he will benefit in that it will be easy for him to fulfill this practice while standing in the synagogue engaged in prayer, when it is not fitting to divert his attention to look beyond four cubits — as we shall elaborate further regarding prayer, please God. The general principle is that a person must fulfill every matter of piety within his own home first, as King David, peace be upon him, said, "I will walk within my heart, within my house" (Psalms 101:2), and afterward it will be easy for him to fulfill it when outside his house. Concerning this King Solomon, peace be upon him, commanded, saying, "Let your eyes look straight ahead, and your eyelids look right before you" (Proverbs 4:25) — the plain sense of the verse being that since the Shechinah is opposite him, it is disgraceful for a servant to look at his master's face.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:24: According to the mystical sense, the reason not to look beyond four cubits is that one must equate his own measure with the measure of his Master — for just as it is written regarding His eyes, blessed be He, "the eyes of the Lord your God are always upon it" (Deuteronomy 11:12), and its measure is four cubits, equal to the number of the four letters of Adonai, so a person must conduct himself accordingly. When a person practices this measure, he unifies the Name YAHDONHY (combined) — for in the eye there is the Name YHVH as explained above, and when he looks at the ground, which is Adonai (see Tikkunei Zohar 84a), he thereby unifies; but if he looks beyond what is needed, he separates YHVH from Adonai, because he is haughty of eye.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:25: The reason in more precise detail is this: as is known, any seed that is deposited within the female is not called "seed in vain," and sight, which is the supernal light emerging from the pupil of the eye — the upper Yod — is like the physical seed emerging from the sign of the Covenant, the lower Yod (Ra'aya Meheimna, Parashat Pinchas 256a); and just as we were commanded not to emit the physical seed in vain, so with sight, one must not emit it in vain — not looking at what he does not need — but rather his eyes should be [directed] to the ground, and then it is not in vain.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:26: And what we say — that one should not look beyond four cubits — means that for most of one's walking he should not look with a full, direct gaze, for then he would be haughty of eye, and it is written, "he who has a haughty eye... him I will not endure" (Psalms 101:5). But if he happens to lift his eyes far off, this is no blemish to his eyes — for perhaps he will see a lost object and return it, and in this sight he performs a mitzvah; and likewise if he sees his teacher from far off, within the distance of "as far as his eyes can see," he must rise before him — this too is a mitzvah, since "you shall rise before the aged" (Leviticus 19:32). Similarly, King David, peace be upon him, said, "I lift up my eyes to the mountains, from where shall my help come" (Psalms 121:1), and in saying "I lift up," it appears that his usual manner of walking was with lowered eyes, since he needed to lift them up when necessary; likewise, "and Abraham lifted up his eyes" (Genesis 22:4), and likewise, "and they lifted up their eyes" (Genesis 37:25).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:27: By this we understand, "I made a covenant with my eyes; how then should I look upon a maid?" (Job 31:1). Its meaning is that just as there is a covenant of the tongue and a covenant of the sexual organ, so there is a covenant regarding the eyes — the reason being that "covenant" (brit) is the mystery of the letter Yod, as explained; and just as one must be careful, regarding the lower covenant, not to emit seed in vain, so regarding the covenant of the eyes — and whoever guards the upper Yod, which is in the pupil of the eye, certainly guards the lower Yod that is in the [sign of the] Covenant. As our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Ketubot 46a), "and you shall guard yourself from every evil thing" (Deuteronomy 23:10) — that one should not fantasize by day and come to impurity by night. And fantasy comes about only through sight, for what one has not seen, how would he fantasize about it? This is likewise because the seed comes from the light of a person's eyes, and whoever guards his sight guards the seed, and whoever blemishes his sight blemishes the seed emerging from the brain and from the lower Yod, as will be further explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:28: One might say that the hint of these two Yods is the two Yods in Aleph [spelled Aleph-Yod-Peh-Aleph], and the Vav between the two Yods is the tongue, which is likewise called "covenant"; and whoever guards these three covenants is bound to YHVH and to His unity, blessed be He, which is the aleph alluded to, indicating oneness. You already know that two Yods and a Vav total twenty-six (26), equal to the numerical value of YHVH; and since he is bound to this unity, no outsider, meaning another power, has any part in him. And if, God forbid, he causes a blemish in one of these three, it is as though he blemished the aleph — since the blemish is found in all three, for spirituality does not divide, but is entirely a complete unity, in the manner they said in the Tikkunim, "whatever has a blemish shall not come near" (Leviticus 21:18). Therefore fortunate is whoever is careful to fulfill these matters, for they are founded on the foundation of the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, and truth shows its own way.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:29: Further, know that according to what is said in the Tikkunim (145b), that the nose is Vav, and according to what was explained above, that each pupil of the eye is Yod, it follows that the nose, Vav, is between two Yods — behold, an Aleph — and when a person is humble of eye, the two Yods are unified through the Vav, and thus YHVH is unified. But if not, God forbid, the Yods withdraw, since there is no Vav between them to unify; and when he is angry, or looks in anger, there is judgment in his eyes — therefore they said (Berachot 58a), "he set his eyes upon him, and judgment ruled, and he became a heap of bones."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:30: Now, since the verse "I made a covenant with my eyes" has come to us, let us say something about it — since it pertains to the discourse we are engaged in, it may be explained according to the plain sense, in light of what we have introduced, that a person must set a boundary for sight, not to look beyond four cubits; this is [the meaning of] "I made a covenant with my eyes" — that is, in the sense of a fixed limit and boundary. And this is what it says, "and how (u'mah) should I look upon a maid?" — meaning: I gain by this, that I will not even have the opportunity of looking, even at a maiden, since I have this aforementioned boundary, it is impossible for me to come to look — this is [the meaning of] "u'mah" ("and how"), for it should have said "and I will not look" [in the future tense], but rather it is as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:31: Further, one might say that just as the [physical] covenant has both circumcision (milah) and uncovering (periah), so with the eyes there is a parallel to the restrictions we shall write about, please God — this being the "milah," which is the foreskin cast outward. However, there are worldly matters one is permitted to look at, provided he recites a blessing — such as one who goes out in the month of Nisan and sees trees blossoming, blessing, "Blessed is He who has such in His world, and has created good creatures" and so on (Berachot 43b) — this person derives enjoyment from seeing a physical thing, but in the blessing he recites over it he encompasses the physical and makes it spiritual; similarly all the things mentioned in the Gemara, chapter HaRo'eh, over which blessings are recited — one who sees the Great Sea (Berachot 9:2). This is the aspect of "periah" — the foreskin included inward into holiness. It follows that, in the pattern of the [physical] covenant, "I made a covenant with my eyes" means that there should be both milah and periah within them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:32: Among the things one must be careful of, some are stated in the Gemara (Avodah Zarah 20b), in these words: "and you shall guard yourself from every evil thing" (Deuteronomy 23:10) — that a person should not look at a beautiful woman, even if unmarried, or at a married woman even if unattractive, or at colored garments of a woman, or at a male donkey or a female donkey, or at a boar or a sow, or at birds while they are mating — so far the Baraita's words. And it further says there in the Gemara: "or at colored garments of a woman" — Rav Yehudah said in the name of Shmuel, even spread out on a wall. Rav Papa said, and this is when he recognizes their owner. Rava said, this is also precise, for it teaches "colored garments of a woman" and not "colored garments," from which we learn [it applies specifically when he knows whose they are] — so far their words. From this Baraita you learn that since they forbade [looking at] a woman's garments spread out on a wall, when one recognizes the woman, all the more so it would be forbidden to look at a bed where a man and his wife sleep, if he recognizes them, for this would arouse desire even more.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:33: Further, we say in tractate Shabbat (64a), regarding the women of Midian, of whom it is written (Numbers 31:50), "and we have brought an offering for the Lord, what every man has found, jewels of gold, chains, and bracelets, rings, earrings...": it was taught in the school of Rabbi Yishmael, why did the men of that generation need atonement? Because they feasted their eyes on the nakedness. Rav Sheshet said, why did the verse enumerate the ornaments worn outwardly together with those worn inwardly? To tell you: whoever looks at a woman's little finger is as though he looked at her private place — so far their words. Rashi explains: outward ornaments — a ring; inward ones — a "kumaz." Whoever looks at the little finger, which is where the ring is worn, is like one who looks at the place of the "kumaz" — this atonement came because they looked. "Kumaz" we say in the Gemara is a mold [ornament] for the shape of the womb.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:34: Further, we say in Bava Batra (57b), on the verse, "and shuts his eyes from looking upon evil" (Isaiah 33:15), in these words: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said, this refers to one who does not look at women while they stand at the washing [place]. How is this to be understood? If there is another path, he is wicked [for going that way anyway]; if there is no other path, he is under duress [and blameless]. Rather, it means when there is no other path, and even so he must force himself [to look away] — so far their words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:35: Further, we say in Nedarim (20a): Rabbi Acha bar Yoshiah says, whoever gazes upon women eventually comes to transgression, and whoever looks at the heel of a woman will have unworthy children. Rav Yosef said, and [this is regarding looking at the heel of] his wife when she is a niddah. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said, "heel" (akeivah) as taught refers to the place of impurity, which is directly opposite the heel — so far their words. And adjacent to this it says there: it was taught, "and that His fear may be upon your faces" (Exodus 20:17) — this refers to shame; "that you sin not" — this teaches that shame brings one to fear of sin, as we quoted in the Gate of Awe, end of chapter 3. The juxtaposition of this Baraita to the matter of looking, and so on, is to teach that one must feel shame before his Maker who looks upon him, and by this he will not come to look at nakedness and at the covered places of his wife that are nakedness, as we say (Berachot 24a), "a woman's leg is nakedness," and so on — for from looking one comes to fantasy, and from fantasy to impurity, and thereby transgresses what is written in the Torah, "and you shall guard yourself from every evil thing" (Deuteronomy 23:10), as we quoted above. It follows that shame brings one to fear of sin, as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:36: Further, they said in the Midrash (Yalkut Kohelet, remez 976), on the verse, "Good before God shall escape from her" (Ecclesiastes 7:26) — this refers to one who sees a woman in bed and flees; "and the sinner shall be caught by her" — this refers to one who is caught with her — so far their words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:37: Further, they said in tractate Megillah (28a) that it is forbidden to look at the face of a wicked person, in these words, on the verse, "were it not that I regard the presence of Jehoshaphat... I would not look toward you, nor see you" (II Kings 3:14): Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai said, it is forbidden to look at the image of a wicked person, as it is said, "I would not look toward you, nor see you." Rabbi Elazar says, [Isaac's] eyes grew dim, as it is said, "and it came to pass that when Isaac was old, and his eyes were dim..." (Genesis 27:1), because he looked at Esau, and it is written, "to accept the face of the wicked is not good" (Proverbs 18:5) — so far their words. And in Sefer Chasidim (siman 826): whoever looks at his wife when she is a niddah, and likewise whoever looks at the face of an angry person, forgets his learning — these are words of wisdom that need no reinforcement of proofs.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:38: And in the Zohar (Parashat Kedoshim 83b) further things are said that one is forbidden to look at; they said, of blessed memory: we have learned, it is forbidden for a person to look at a woman's beauty, so as not to come to an evil fantasy and be uprooted toward another matter. And so Rabbi Shimon used to do: when he walked in the town and his colleagues walked behind him, and he saw beautiful women, he would lower his eyes and say to his colleagues, "Do not turn" (Leviticus 19:4). And whoever looks at a woman's beauty by day comes to fantasy at night, and if that evil fantasy arises upon him, he transgresses because of [the verse], "nor make for yourselves molten gods" (Leviticus 19:4). Further, if he has relations with his wife at a time when that evil fantasy has arisen upon him, the children born from that are called "molten gods." "Do not turn to idols, nor make for yourselves molten gods." Rabbi Abba said, it is forbidden for a person to look at the idols of the nations, or to derive benefit from them, or to be healed by them, and all the more so to look at them, for it is forbidden for a person to look at a place that is not needed — so far their words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:39: From this you can see the severity of the prohibition against looking — from what it says at the end of its words, "and all the more so to look at them," [showing] there is more prohibition in looking than in being healed by them, and it gives the reason: because it is forbidden for a person to look at a place he does not need. The reason is that he thereby diverts his mind from holiness to something vain and empty, in the manner of what they expounded (Shabbat 149a-b), "do not turn to idols" — "do not turn from your own knowledge" — for anything a person does not need to look at, yet looks at anyway, is an "outsider" (chitzoni), since "outsider" refers to what a person does not need, which is the refuse of holiness. And so it says in the Zohar (Parashat Pekudei 263a) that the evil inclination entices a person to look at what he does not need and to satiate his eyes with the matters of this world, in order to break his eyes in the grave for every single sight; and any external thing that becomes portrayed in his thought upon looking causes a blemish in the neshamah clothed there, as explained above — and it will not seem far-fetched when you see how many supernal mysteries are in the eye, according to what we have quoted from the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:40: It follows, as a general rule, that whoever looks at what is not needed transgresses both a positive and a negative commandment — "turn from evil" and "do good" — for by diverting his mind from holiness he transgresses the positive commandment, and by acquiring in his soul the form of that evil thing, this is the negative commandment.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:41: Besides this, it is forbidden to look at anything that would bring a person to joy [at an inappropriate time], as is said in the Zohar (Parashat Tazria 45b), in these words: Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Yosei were walking on the road; when they reached a certain field, they saw a certain "petira dekitfa" (a tree of balsam) on the right side of the road. Rabbi Yosei said, a covering of smoke is upon our eyes; we should not see it in joy, since the day the Temple was destroyed — so far his words. The explanation of "a covering of smoke" is a covering, tie, or smoke [screen] over the eyes, and the intent is the concealment of the eyes so as not to see with joy.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:42: Further, it says there (Parashat Kedoshim 84a): come and see, it is forbidden for a person to look at a place that the Holy One, blessed be He, despises and that His soul is distant from; and if it is forbidden to look at what the Holy One, blessed be He, loves, how much more so at what He distances Himself from. And come and see, it is forbidden for a person to look at a rainbow, because it is a vision of the supernal image; it is forbidden for a person to look at his own sign of the Covenant, because it alludes to the Righteous One of the world. It is forbidden for a person to look at the fingers of the priests at the time they spread their hands [in the priestly blessing], because there the glory of the supernal King rests. And if it is forbidden to look at a supernal holy place, how much more so at a distant, impure place! Therefore, "Do not turn to idols" — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:43: Further, there (Parashat Beshalach 66b), in these words: it is forbidden to look at the rainbow — which rainbow? Rabbi Abba said, the rainbow simply. What is "the rainbow simply"? He said to him: both the rainbow above and the rainbow below. The rainbow above is in its colors, for whoever looks at its colors is as though he looked at the supernal place, and it is forbidden to look at it lest one demean the Shechinah. The rainbow below — what is it? That sign of the Covenant marked upon a person, for whoever looks at it demeans [that which is] above. Rabbi Yitzchak said, if so, is it not written, "Put, I pray you, your hand under my thigh" (Genesis 24:2), where he would swear by this sign? He said to him, leave the Patriarchs of the world aside, for they are not like other people; and further, it says "put your hand under my thigh" and not "look under my thigh." Therefore it is forbidden to look at the rainbow simply, as we have learned — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:44: And in the Midrash (Kohelet Rabbah 9:11) it says that Rabbeinu HaKadosh (Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi) was so called because he never looked at his own [sign of the Covenant] in his life. Antoninus said to him, "When you make a [ritual] cut, do you look at what you are cutting?" He said to him, "On my own I have never looked in my life, but on yours I will look" — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:45: And in tractate Chagigah, on what is said in the Mishnah (2:1), "whoever does not have regard for the honor of his Maker, it would have been better for him not to have come into the world" — they say in the Gemara (16a): what does this refer to? Rabbi Abba said, this refers to one who looks at the rainbow; Rav Yosef said, this refers to one who commits a transgression in secret. [Regarding] one who looks at the rainbow, as it is written, "as the appearance of the bow that is in the cloud in the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness round about, this was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the Lord" (Ezekiel 1:28) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:46: The punishment for one who blemishes his sight is explained in the Zohar, Parashat Pekudei (263a), in one of the chambers of impurity. They said, of blessed memory: beneath this officer stands another officer, having a thousand and ten thousand under him, and this officer is called "Pattot" (Enticer) — he is the one appointed to entice people, and he presides over them and leads them astray to look at and gaze upon what they do not need, in many kinds of harlotry and adulteries; and all those with him stand near him and go before him and force him to divert his eyes to look at what is not needed. This is Sarsurim, who is an evil broker for all these evils; he stands over the grave from the time that body is judged, and he breaks its eyes, because he is the one they profited from while in this world, and they belong to him; and there the soul is judged in this place until it enters that place called "Bor" (Pit), where there are many snakes and scorpions that all sting that soul and take hold of it and judge it — so far their words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:47: The reason the punishment for one who blemishes his sight is in this first chamber, and not in the other chambers, seems to me to be that whoever blemishes his sight blemishes the Shechinah, who is the pupil of the eye, from where light emerges; therefore, in contrast to her is the cleansing of the neshamah from the blemish. And everything they said, "and you shall guard yourself from every evil thing," that one should not look, and so on, is because in looking at an evil thing he draws upon himself the powers of Lilith that spread from this chamber — for "evil" (ra) is Samael, and "an evil thing" is Lilith and her powers, which are the causes of bringing a person to become evil (ra), spilling seed in vain, which is called "evil" — and therefore his own powers, through which he sinned, are the ones that exact punishment, in the manner explained in the Zohar (Parashat Korach 177a), "for the work of a man He rewards him" (Job 34:11).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:48: Because the blemish of sight is so great, as we have elaborated, we find in the Midrash that Rabbi Matya ben Charash drove pins into his eyes so as not to stumble. It is said in the Midrash quoted in Yalkut (Parashat Vayechi, remez 161), on the verse, "Joseph is a fruitful bough" (Genesis 49:22): a story of Rabbi Matya ben Charash, who was sitting in the study hall and occupied with Torah, and the radiance of his face was like the sun, and his facial features were like those of ministering angels, for he had never in his life raised his eyes to a woman in the world. Once Satan passed by and became jealous of him; he said, "Is it possible that a person like this has never sinned?" He said before the Holy One, blessed be He, "Master of the universe, what is Rabbi Matya ben Charash before You?" He said to him, "He is completely righteous." He said before Him, "Give me permission and I will entice him." He said to him, "You cannot [overcome] him." [Satan said,] "Nevertheless." He said to him, "Go." He appeared to him as a woman more beautiful than any that had ever been in her form, since the days of Naamah, the sister of Tubal-Cain, at whom the ministering angels erred, as it is said, "and the sons of God saw the daughters of men" (Genesis 6:2). She stood before him; once he saw her, he turned his face and put it behind him. She came again and stood at his left side; he turned his face to the right. She kept turning to face him from every side. He said, "I am afraid the evil inclination will overpower me and cause me to sin." What did that righteous man do? He called the student who was serving him and said, "Go and bring me fire and pins." He brought him pins and he thrust them into his eyes. When Satan saw this, he trembled and fell backward. At that hour the Holy One, blessed be He, called Raphael and said to him, "Go and heal Rabbi Matya ben Charash." He came and stood before him. [Rabbi Matya] said to him, "Who are you?" He said to him, "I am Raphael, whom the Holy One, blessed be He, sent to heal your eyes." He said to him, "Leave me; what has happened has happened." [Raphael] returned before the Holy One, blessed be He, and said before Him, "Master of the universe, this is what Matya said to me." He said to him, "Go and tell him, I guarantee that the evil inclination will not rule over him." Immediately he healed him. From here the Sages said: whoever does not look at women, and all the more so at his fellow's wife, the evil inclination does not rule over him — so far their words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:49: Now, having discussed the blemish of the eyes, let us discuss their rectification. It is a mitzvah to look with one's eyes at the creations of the Creator, as David said, "When I consider Your heavens, the work of Your fingers, the moon and the stars which You have established, what is man that You are mindful of him" (Psalms 8:4-5). Likewise, to look at the commandment of tzitzit, as it is said, "and you shall see it and remember..." (Numbers 15:39). Likewise, if he sees a Torah scroll, or a sage, or an elder passing before him, he should rise before him and honor him according to his obligation, and not avert his eyes so as not to see him and rise — for concerning this it is said, in this commandment, "you shall rise before the aged... and you shall fear your God" (Leviticus 19:32). And in Sefer Chasidim it is written that if one was sitting and saw an elder [approaching], he should stand up before he reaches him, so that when he passes before him the standing be for the sake of the mitzvah and not by chance [as though standing for another reason].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:50: Rabbeinu Yonah, peace be upon him, wrote in Sha'arei Teshuvah (Gate 1, siman 15) that whoever has sinned with his eyes, his rectification is to shed tears with his eyes over his sins, as King David, peace be upon him, said, "Rivers of water run down my eyes, because they [the people/eyes] have not kept Your Torah" (Psalms 119:136) — it does not say "because I have not kept Your Torah," but "because they have not kept" — the intent being, because the eyes did not keep Your Torah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:51: Among the rectifications of the eyes is to shed tears over a worthy person, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said in tractate Shabbat (105a), on the verse, "You count my wanderings; put my tears in Your bottle; are they not in Your book?" (Psalms 56:9): Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi said in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, in the name of Bar Kappara: whoever sheds tears over a worthy person, the Holy One, blessed be He, counts them and places them in His treasure house, as it is said, "put my tears in Your bottle, are they not in Your book" — so far their words. And in the Zohar (Parashat Acharei Mot, end of 57a), in these words: and whoever grieves over the loss of the righteous, or sheds tears over them, the Holy One, blessed be He, proclaims concerning him, "and your iniquity is removed, and your sin atoned" (Isaiah 6:7), and not only that, but his children will not die in his days, and concerning him it is written, "he shall see his seed, he shall prolong his days" (Isaiah 53:10) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:52: Rabbeinu Tam wrote in Sefer HaYashar (Gate 4, siman 50) that the rectification of the eyes is that one should rise at the [pre-dawn] watch and not sleep the whole night. It seems to me that David alluded to this in saying, "My eyes anticipate the watches, that I might meditate on Your word" (Psalms 119:148), in the manner of "Rivers of water run down my eyes," which Rabbeinu Yonah explains — the intent being that the eyes that have sinned should drive away sleep from themselves and anticipate the watch to occupy themselves with Torah. I found support for this in the Tikkunim (145a), in these words: and eyes that shine with Torah, of them it is said, "the eyes of all wait upon You, and You give them their food in due season" (Psalms 145:15); and a person must occupy himself with them constantly, evening, morning, and noon (twice daily), [as] the Holy One, blessed be He, [does] — this is what is written, "the eyes of the Lord your God are always upon it, from the beginning of the year even unto the end of the year" (Deuteronomy 11:12) — and we learn "always" from "always": the "always" of evening and morning [prayer/Torah study] to the "always" of "the eyes of the Lord your God are always upon it" — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:53: It seems to me that the rectification of the eyes is likewise in a person's looking with them to read Torah — particularly the Written Torah, and particularly, most especially, when he is called up to read from the Torah scroll in the synagogue.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:54: Further, Rabbeinu Tam wrote (Sefer HaYashar, ibid.) that one's eyes should be closed during prayer, and that he should place his tefillin between his eyes. Now what he says regarding closing the eyes during prayer refers specifically to the Amidah, which is a standing prayer, as is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Va'etchanan 260b), in these words: come and see, whoever stands in prayer must direct his feet, as they have established, and must cover his head as one who sits before a king, and must cover his eyes so as not to look at the Shechinah. And in the book of Rav Hamnuna Sabba it says: whoever opens his eyes during prayer, or does not lower his eyes to the ground, the Angel of Death is summoned against him in advance, and when his soul departs, he shall not look at the light of the Shechinah nor die by a [divine] kiss; whoever demeans the Shechinah is himself demeaned at the hour he needs it — this is what is written, "for those who honor Me I will honor, and those who despise Me shall be lightly esteemed" (I Samuel 2:30). This one who looks at the Shechinah at the time he prays — but how can he look at the Shechinah [literally]? Rather, he should certainly know that the Shechinah stands before him — this is what is written, "and Hezekiah turned his face to the wall" (Isaiah 38:2), for there the Shechinah rested; therefore he need not have any partition between him and the wall — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:55: The rest of his wording, saying "and must cover his eyes," it appears that ideally one should cover his eyes with the tallit of the mitzvah upon him — since it does not say that he should not open his eyes, as it says afterward regarding one who opens his eyes or does not lower them, and below regarding the punishment. Therefore it says that if, at the very least, he does not lower his eyes even if they are open, or he closes them but does not [also properly] lower them even though they are not open, he is punished — but the best manner is that he cover them. This is what I have seen practiced by pious sages — the pious sage Rabbi Elazar ibn Yochai, peace be upon him, and my teacher, peace be upon him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:56: For the rest of the order of prayer, it is good that he lower his eyes so as not to look beyond four cubits — a matter a person is obligated to fulfill always, and at the very least he should not transgress this rectification of being humble of eye during prayer, for if he is haughty of eye, he pushes the Shechinah away from him, as it is written, "he who has a haughty eye... him I will not endure" (Psalms 101:5) — and how could his intention in prayer be proper if the Shechinah is not with him?
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:57: My teacher, peace be upon him, wrote regarding "and you shall not go astray after your heart" (Numbers 15:39) a matter relevant to this discourse, and I saw fit to quote the sum of his words here. In brief, his words are: that anything entering through sight is physical, and therefore a person must close his eyes during prayer, for by removing his eyes from physical things he will think of spiritual things; and this is [the meaning of] "and you shall not go astray after your [physical] heart and your [physical] eyes," but rather after My heart and My eyes, which are the supernal sefirot — "after which you go astray" — for it is a person's natural way, from the side of his soul, to be drawn after the fine spiritual things, and when he thinks of the physical, he is outside his nature, like a harlot (zonah), who is called such because she does what is outside the way of her nature. Therefore a person must purify his thoughts, for just as he would be ashamed to commit a transgression because of shame before the Creator, so he should be ashamed before Him to be seen thinking something against His will, for the thought is revealed before Him just like the deed, as it says, "I the Lord search the heart, I try the reins" (Jeremiah 17:10) — thus far the sum of his words on this matter.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:58: With this introduction we understand what we say in the Sabbath prayer liturgy, in "Vay'chulu Finu" (Would that our mouths...), "for every eye waits upon You" — the intent being that the eye was not built to gaze at physical things, but to be like the eyes of the prophets who gazed at the supernal chariot in those spiritual visions; and this is attained only through closing the eye and concealing it from physical things, as explained, and likewise through guarding the eye from things that blemish it. Therefore the early pious ones were called "open-eyed" (pekichei einayin), as is found in the Zohar in several Tosefta passages (Parashat Yitro 74a); the reason is that they merited proper sight to the point that there was no screen dividing between them and holiness. Among these you will find Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon, peace be upon him, in the story of the gentile who took a purse, and so on, of whom it is said that he could see with his eye all things even from afar (Tosefta 4-58b). Similarly regarding the wisdom of physiognomy, explained in Parashat Yitro (Zohar Parashat Yitro from 70a), that the twenty-two letters are portrayed on the forehead, and through them the wise see. And similarly Rav Hamnuna, who used to sit on Sabbath eve to see the delight of the souls, these ascending and those descending, in Parashat Terumah (see 136b). Concerning something like this they said in tractate Derech Eretz (ch. 4), in these words: your eyes, which you have not set on money that is not yours, shall give you light in the pupil of darkness and gloom, as it is said, "and your light shall shine in darkness" (Isaiah 58:10) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:59: Regarding the greatness of one who guards his sight and does not follow after what his eyes see, they said in tractate Kallah (ch. 2), in these words: Rabbi Yochai bar Yoshiyahu said, whoever gazes at women eventually comes to transgression; and whoever removes himself from a transgression and does not commit it, even if he is an ordinary Israelite, deserves to offer a burnt offering upon the altar like a High Priest, as it is said, "and he sent the young men of the children of Israel, and they offered burnt offerings" (Exodus 24:5). And whoever makes himself lazy [i.e., restrains himself] from a transgression and does not commit it is sustained by the splendor of the Shechinah like the ministering angels, as it is said, "and they beheld God, and did eat and drink" (Exodus 24:11) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:60: Further, they said, of blessed memory, in Bava Batra (see Vayikra Rabbah 23:13): Rabbi Miyasha, grandson of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, [said]: whoever sees a matter of nakedness and does not feast his eyes on it merits to receive the presence of the Shechinah. What is the reason? "He shuts his eyes from looking upon evil" (Isaiah 33:15); what is written after it? "Your eyes shall see the King in His beauty" (Isaiah 33:17) — so far their words. The reason that receiving the presence of the Shechinah [is the reward] for guarding one's sight is simple, according to what we have explained above — that a matter of nakedness (ervah) is an outsider, [as] a matter of ervah certainly — and every ervah is Resh-Ayin, Vav-Heh, as explained in the Tikkunim (99a). Since this person guards himself so as not to separate the union of Vav-Heh, he deserves to receive the presence of the Shechinah, for the presence of the Shechinah is the [state of] unification, as will be further explained below, please God. This is [the meaning of] "the King in His beauty" — rather, the intent is in the mystery of unification, that is, the sixth attribute [Yesod], in which is the mystery of beauty, and likewise the ninth attribute [likewise Yesod, per another counting], as in "and Joseph was of beautiful form" (Genesis 39:6) — and this is what was explained at the beginning of the chapter, that by blemishing sight one blemishes the pupil of the eye and the light of the pupil of the eye; and since he did not blemish them and was saved, he rectified the supernal unification, and therefore his soul will merit to receive the illumination of the supernal unification. With this, the matter of the rectification of the eyes and the greatness of guarding them properly is concluded.
